items.prompt: What is the difference between the precise word and the general word, and what does the reader get from each?
items.canonical_answer: The precise word names the exact thing — a jackal, trotting — and the reader sees one animal at one speed; the general word gestures at a family of things — an animal, moving quickly — and the reader must build the picture the writer left unbuilt. The reader gets a sighting from the first and a category from the second, and the difference is the work the reader has to do.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: the exact thing named against a family gestured at.
Must say what the reader gets from each — the built picture against the build-it-yourself kit.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is a sentence of general words: "The man went quickly to the big building because there was a bad problem." Rewrite it with precise words, keeping the content.
items.canonical_answer: A rewrite: "The caretaker jogged to the boiler house because the pipe had burst." (Any rewrite that names the man, the speed, the building and the problem exactly keeps the content and gives the reader the picture: the test is whether each general word has become one exact thing.)
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: the words of the general sentence made precise, because the words are the proof.
The strongest answers name all four — the man, the speed, the building, the problem — so nothing is left as a category.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is a context: "The fire spread through the dry grass, helped by a wind that changed its mind three times." Choose between these three words for the space — "moved", "sprinted", "edged" — and give the reason.
items.canonical_answer: "Sprinted" is the choice: fire in dry grass with a changing wind moves fast and unevenly, and "sprinted" carries both the speed and the suddenness of the direction changes. "Moved" is too general to earn its place, and "edged" says slow and steady, which contradicts the dry grass and the wind the sentence names. (Any choice with a reason drawn from the context’s own words does the job; the reason is the skill.)
marking_guidance: Credit the choice with its reason drawn from the words of the context.
The strongest answers test each rejected word against the context and say why it fails, so the choice shows.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What does a range of language mean, and what is it measured in?
items.canonical_answer: It means varied vocabulary, sentence structures and literary features — all controlled. It is measured in what the writing keeps accurate, not in what it attempts: a range the writer cannot hold is not range but risk, and the syllabus asks for ideas expressed clearly, coherently and accurately with an appropriate range, which makes accuracy the measure and the range the reward for passing it.
marking_guidance: Credit the features: varied vocabulary, structures and devices, all controlled.
The measure — what stays accurate — is what stops range becoming a liability.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The team’s victory was a pyrrhic one, which was very nice for everyone." What has gone wrong, and what is the rule?
items.canonical_answer: The ambitious word is used in the wrong sense: a pyrrhic victory is one won at ruinous cost, and "very nice for everyone" contradicts it in the same breath — the reader who knows the word winces, and the reader who does not is misled. The rule is that an unusual word must be a word the writer can use, not just find: use the range you own, own the range you use, and check each new word’s sense before it carries a sentence.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the ambitious word used against its own sense.
Must give the rule: the word owned before it is used, its sense checked before it carries a sentence.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Why does control come before complexity in the writing marks?
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that the range is judged inside accuracy: the table rewards expression the writer keeps command of, and a sentence the writer can hold is worth ten the writer cannot, because the held sentence communicates and the unheld one buries its meaning in its own grammar. Complexity is only range when it is controlled — otherwise it is the error wearing a decoration.
marking_guidance: Credit the reason: range is judged inside accuracy, so command is what gets credited.
An answer about "showing off" has described the risk, not the mechanism.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is an overlong sentence that has lost control: "The bus, which had been waiting since dawn, its engine idling in the cold while the driver drank tea in the cafe whose lights were the only ones on in the street, finally, when everyone had given up, left." Rewrite it as two clear sentences.
items.canonical_answer: A rewrite: "The bus had been waiting since dawn, its engine idling in the cold, while the driver drank tea in the cafe — the only lights on in the street. When everyone had given up, it finally left." (Any two sentences that keep the content and give each clause a verb that can find its subject does the job: the split at the natural break is the skill.)
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: the overlong sentence split at its natural break, because the words show the control.
The strongest answers keep every fact and lose every stranded clause, so the content survives and the grammar does too.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a varied range of sentences and long sentences that lose control?
items.canonical_answer: A varied range is different shapes held deliberately — simple, compound, complex, minor, fronted — each chosen for its effect and each surviving its own grammar. Long sentences that lose control are range attempted and lost: the clause that cannot find its verb takes the meaning down with it, and the reader is left at the moment of the writer’s highest ambition. The test is survival: read the sentence aloud, and if the breath and the grammar give out together, the sentence was never held.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: shapes chosen and held against length attempted and lost.
Must give the test: the sentence survives its own grammar — the read-aloud check is the cleanest form.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A draft reads: "Although the rain had stopped, the river, which had been rising since Tuesday, was still climbing, and the bridge, which the council had inspected in March and had declared safe, and which everyone used, was, the warden said, in his opinion, at risk." What has gone wrong, and what is the fix?
items.canonical_answer: The grammar has broken under the ambition: the bridge’s clause cannot find its way back to its verb (“was… at risk” is reached through two stacked relative clauses and three interruptions), and the reader loses the sentence at its centre. The fix is the split: the facts become three sentences — the rain, the river, the bridge and its inspection, and the warden’s warning — and each fact lands before the next one is carried. The control marks read the attempt as the error, which is exactly what the table rewards: expression kept in command, not ambition left dangling.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the clause that cannot find its verb, lost under stacked interruption.
Must give the fix: the split into sentences that each land, so the ambition is served rather than buried.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is a comma splice, and how is it fixed?
items.canonical_answer: A comma splice is two complete sentences joined by a comma alone — "the gates opened at six, the crowd was already waiting" — and it is fixed three ways: a full stop makes two sentences, a semicolon joins two that belong together, or a conjunction with its comma does the joining the comma cannot.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: two complete sentences joined by a comma alone.
All three fixes are worth credit, because the splice has three honest repairs.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is a comma splice: "The storm took the roof off the kitchen, we cooked in the fireplace for a week." Correct it in three different ways.
items.canonical_answer: First: a full stop — "The storm took the roof off the kitchen. We cooked in the fireplace for a week." Second: a semicolon — "The storm took the roof off the kitchen; we cooked in the fireplace for a week." Third: a conjunction — "The storm took the roof off the kitchen, so we cooked in the fireplace for a week." Each repair keeps both sentences whole and gives the joining an honest tool.
marking_guidance: Credit all three corrections in the words: the full stop, the semicolon, the conjunction.
Each repair is the same splice fixed with a different honest tool, so two is half the card.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between an accidental sentence fragment and a deliberate minor sentence, and what is the test?
items.canonical_answer: An accidental fragment is an error: a subordinate clause with nothing to belong to — "Because the gates opened." — left holding a sentence’s position. A deliberate minor sentence is a choice: "Not this time." — held for effect, with the writing around it showing the decision. The test is the question each fragment is asked in the proofread: did the writer decide this? If the grammar broke, it goes; if the effect was chosen, it stays — and the writer is the only one who knows which.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: the grammar broke against the writer decided.
Must give the test: the proofread’s question to each fragment, decided or broken.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: State the rules for punctuating and paragraphing direct speech.
items.canonical_answer: The marks go around the words actually spoken. The reporting clause — she said, he asked — takes its comma inside the marks when it follows the speech (“There it is,” she said) and a comma before the opening mark when it leads (She said, “there it is”). A new paragraph begins for each new speaker, and the narrative around the speech punctuates normally: the sentence’s own end mark sits inside the closing speech mark if it belongs to the speech, outside if it belongs to the reporting.
marking_guidance: Credit the features: marks around the words, the reporting clause and its comma, new paragraph per speaker.
The inside-or-outside placement of end marks is the rule the answer should reach.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is a passage with tense shifts: "The market opened at six. The first customers arrive before the stalls are ready. The seller waved them away, but they come back at seven with baskets." Correct the tense so the passage stands in one time.
items.canonical_answer: A corrected version: "The market opened at six. The first customers arrived before the stalls were ready. The seller waved them away, but they came back at seven with baskets." (Every verb is checked against the past the opening chose: arrive/arrived, are/were, come/came — and the proofread’s second pass is exactly this, verb by verb.)
marking_guidance: Credit the corrections in the words: each shifted verb brought back to the chosen tense.
The chosen tense is decided first and every verb checked against it, so the fix shows the method.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is a passage with capital errors: "we met at the okavango river lodge on thursday. my sister Kauna had booked it, and even the manager, mr tshisevhe, was surprised by how many of us arrived from Oshakati." Correct the capitals.
items.canonical_answer: A corrected version: "We met at the Okavango River Lodge on Thursday. My sister Kauna had booked it, and even the manager, Mr Tshisevhe, was surprised by how many of us arrived from Oshakati." (Sentence openings, the establishment’s name, the day, and the honorific with its surname all take capitals; Oshakati already had its own.)
marking_guidance: Credit the corrections: sentence openings, the proper nouns and the honorific, in the words of the passage.
The strongest answers name the categories they fixed, so the pass shows the rule and not just the fixes.

items.prompt: What is the difference between its and it’s, and how do you check which one a sentence needs?
items.canonical_answer: Its is possessive — the river and its bridge — and it’s is the contraction of it is or it has: the apostrophe stands for the missing letters. The check is the expansion: read the sentence with "it is" where the word sits, and if the sentence survives, the contraction is right; if it collapses, the possessive is. "It’s a long river" survives as "it is"; "the river and it’s bridge" does not, so it wants its.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: possessive against contraction, with the apostrophe’s job.
Must give the check: the expansion to "it is", which settles every case.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between their, there and they’re, and what is the check for each?
items.canonical_answer: Their is possessive — their bus; there is place — over there, there it is; and they’re is the contraction of they are. The checks: their expands to nothing but possession (whose? theirs), there points (where? there), and they’re expands (they are — does the sentence still hold?). Each word answers a different question, and the question is the check.
marking_guidance: Must state all three: possession, place, contraction.
Must give the checks — whose, where, the expansion — so the difference is usable, not just named.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give the proofreading passes, in order, and say why one error per pass works.
items.canonical_answer: First pass: sentence boundaries — splices and fragments. Second pass: agreement and tense — the verb against its subject, the tense against its neighbours. Third pass: capitals and proper nouns, speech punctuation, and the small rest. One error per pass works because the finding is what takes the time: a pass with one thing to look for finds it, and a vague read looking for everything finds little — which is why three focused reads are faster than one general one.
marking_guidance: Credit the three passes in order: boundaries, agreement and tense, capitals and the rest.
The reason — one thing at a time is findable — is what makes the order worth having.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner’s draft reads: "The queue was long, people gave up, I stayed. After an hour the doors opens and everyone rushes forward, then stopped." Name the two errors, and give the fix for each.
items.canonical_answer: The first error is the comma splice — "The queue was long, people gave up, I stayed" is three complete sentences joined by commas — fixed with full stops or semicolons: "The queue was long; people gave up; I stayed." The second is tense drift — "opens" and "rushes" are present in a passage standing in the past, and "stopped" swings back — fixed by choosing the past and checking every verb: "After an hour the doors opened and everyone rushed forward, then stopped." Both errors are first-pass and second-pass errors in the proofread’s order, which is why the order exists.
marking_guidance: Must name both errors, each named as an error: the splice and the tense drift, in the draft’s words.
Must give both fixes, and the note that the proofread’s passes would have caught each in turn.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A story opens in the past — "The night the lights failed, my mother lit the stove" — and by the third paragraph reads "The stove gives the only light in the kitchen. I watch her face." What has happened, and what is the proofread’s fix?
items.canonical_answer: The tense has drifted from past to present, and the reader has lost the sense of when the piece stands: the opening promised a memory and the third paragraph delivers a live scene, and the effect reads as error rather than choice. The proofread’s fix is the second pass — choose one tense, then check every verb against it — unless the historic present is a deliberate whole-text decision, in which case the opening must join it. The one thing a piece cannot do is stand in both: the drift is the error, and the choice must be made on purpose.
marking_guidance: Must name what happened: the drift from past to present, read as error not choice.
Must give the fix: one tense chosen and every verb checked — or the whole piece moved deliberately.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A draft’s paragraph has no capitals at three sentence openings, and one sentence that reads "And went to the gate." What has gone wrong, and what does each error cost?
items.canonical_answer: Three sentence openings have lost their capitals — the small, visible errors that are cheap to fix and costly in the impression they leave, because they signal to the reader that no final pass happened. And "And went to the gate." is an accidental fragment: a verb with no subject, broken rather than decided — the proofread’s first pass would ask it "did I decide this?", get no for an answer, and give it a subject or a full stop. Each error costs little alone; together they cost the accuracy strand its level, which is the price of skipping the passes.
marking_guidance: Must name both errors, each named as an error: the missing capitals and the accidental fragment, in the draft’s words.
Must say what each costs — the impression of no final pass, and the accuracy strand’s level.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A story’s dialogue reads: "Where is it she said I looked everywhere and he said try the kitchen she said nothing and he left." What has gone wrong, and what is the repair?
items.canonical_answer: The speech has been run into the narrative without its punctuation or new paragraphs: no quotation marks, no reporting commas, and no paragraph breaks — so who said what is a crowd, and the reader cannot tell the two speakers apart. The repair is the full rule set: marks around the words actually spoken, the reporting clause with its comma, and a new paragraph for each new speaker — "Where is it?" she said. / "I looked everywhere." / He said, "Try the kitchen." / She said nothing, and he left." — and the conversation becomes a dialogue instead of a brawl.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: speech run in without marks, commas or new paragraphs.
Must give the repair: the three rules applied, so the speakers separate and the conversation reads.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt:
Proofread this passage. It contains three comma splices and three capital-letter errors (sentence openings and one proper noun), and one agreement error.

"The rain had stopped by dawn, the river was still rising. the water came up the bank and into the maize. we ran to the cattle pen with the rope. By seven the water was in the yard, it had reached the step, the whole family was on the veranda. my grandmother said the flood of 1972 was higher. she was calm, and the rest of us was not. the boat came at noon, it took the children first. we watched the water go down all night. by friday the sun was back, and the mud was everywhere, but the house stood."

The corrected passage is the answer.
items.canonical_answer:
The rain had stopped by dawn; the river was still rising. The water came up the bank and into the maize. We ran to the cattle pen with the rope. By seven the water was in the yard; it had reached the step, and the whole family was on the veranda. My grandmother said the flood of 1972 was higher. She was calm, and the rest of us were not. The boat came at noon, and it took the children first. We watched the water go down all night. By Friday the sun was back, and the mud was everywhere, but the house stood.
(The passage carried three comma splices, two missing capitals at sentence openings, one agreement error — ‘the rest of us was’ — and a missing capital on a proper noun, ‘friday’; the correction fixes each, and the passes that found them were boundaries, then agreement and tense, then capitals.)
marking_guidance: Credit the corrected passage: every named kind of error found and fixed, because the words are the proof.
Credit the method: the passes run in order — boundaries, then agreement and tense, then capitals and the rest — so the effect of the correction is each pass finding its own errors.
The model passage is the standard: three splices fixed, the capitals and the proper noun restored, the agreement corrected — every error named in the prompt found and fixed.

items.prompt:
Here is a flat descriptive paragraph of about 100 words:

"The dune field is beautiful. It is big and orange and bright and wide. The sand goes on for a long way. The sun makes it hot. There are plants and animals and insects and things. It is quiet. The quietness of the quiet dunes is very quiet. In the evening the colours of the sand change to different colours and the light makes it look like something from a painting in a gallery that you might see."

Rewrite it with precise vocabulary and controlled, varied sentences. A model rewrite is the answer.
items.canonical_answer:
The dune field is enormous: it runs east for three ridges, each one higher than the road. By four the sun has turned it the colour of a struck match head, and the shadows of the three oryx on the far crest lie across the sand like separate dunes. Between the ridges the wind has written the day’s whole history in ridges and shallows, and the only sound is the sand itself — a soft ticking under the wind, the desert doing its arithmetic. In the evening the light goes low and the field becomes a different country: the orange turns to rust, the crests catch fire, and for ten minutes the place looks like a painting of itself.
(The original paragraph had stacked adjectives where precision was owed — ‘big and orange and bright and wide’ — repeated phrasing — the quietness of the quiet dunes — and a simile that trailed off into vagueness; the rewrite replaces each with one exact thing and varied, controlled sentence shapes, and the words show the range the rewrite claims.)
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: precise words replacing the stacked general ones, because the words are the proof.
Credit the controlled variety: different sentence shapes held deliberately, so the effect of the rewrite is range kept inside accuracy.
The model rewrite is the standard: one exact thing where the original gestured at a family, and sentence shapes the writer can hold.

items.prompt:
Here is a ranting argument paragraph of about 100 words:

"I think that school uniforms are bad. They are uncomfortable and they cost money and they make everyone look the same which is boring. Some people say they are good. But they are wrong. Uniforms are a thing of the past and the past is bad. Also they are itchy. Everyone I know agrees with me and my cousin said they are the worst. So uniforms should be abolished now and forever."

Rewrite it with precise vocabulary, controlled and varied sentences, and a persuasive register — keeping the position. A model rewrite is the answer.
items.canonical_answer:
Uniforms, I will grant, solve one real problem: the morning argument about clothes, which every parent has lost. But the solution is bought at three costs the argument keeps ignoring. They are expensive — the full set costs a month of many families’ food budget, and it is worn five days a week, which makes it the most expensive garment per wear in the house. They are uncomfortable in this climate — a polyester shirt in February is a small act of cruelty, and learning while cooked is learning anyway, but why. And they teach conformity as a value, quietly, by the only method a school has: repetition. My cousin, who has worn one for four years, calls it ‘the worst thing about the worst day of the week’, and she is thirteen, which is the age the argument is supposedly for. There are other ways to solve the morning argument — a dress code, a colour scheme, a rule about slogans — and the abolition of the uniform deserves a better answer than ‘it has always been this way’.
(The original paragraph ranted — assertion stacked on assertion, ‘some people say… but they are wrong’ without a case — and repeated instead of developing; the rewrite keeps the position, adds reasons, a specific example and a concession, and recruits the reader with ‘I will grant’ instead of blaming them with ‘they are wrong’.)
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: the position kept, the rant replaced by reasons and a concession, because the words are the proof.
Credit the register: measured and persuasive, so the effect on the reader is recruitment rather than defence.
The model rewrite is the standard: development where the original repeated, and range held inside control.
